title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
1 The failure, again

Same failure as your homework, on new data: Luxembourg
Elevation raster + 12 cantons (districts), both included with terra
Scenario: the national mapping agency sends the elevation in its own national grid



Show code
library(sf)       # vector data
library(terra)    # raster data
library(dplyr)    # filter() and friends
library(spData)   # the `world` dataset, used in section 4
library(units)    # converting m^2 to km^2, used in section 4




Show code
# Elevation raster for Luxembourg
elev_file <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
elev <- rast(elev_file)

# The 12 cantons of Luxembourg, as sf polygons
cantons_file <- system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra")
cantons <- st_read(cantons_file)

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
section: 6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
text:
6 Back to the failure: fix it and check it
Why it failed

Cantons: coordinates around 6 and 50 (degrees)
Raster: coordinates in the tens of thousands (meters)
plot() just draws numbers: cantons landed far outside the raster’s extent
crop(): no overlap → stops
extract(): no cells inside any polygon → NaN, silently

The fix

Put both layers in one CRS
Transform the vector to match the raster: moving vertices is exact, while reprojecting a raster resamples cell values



Show code
# Convert the cantons into the raster's CRS
cantons_lux <- st_transform(cantons, crs(elev_lux))

# Check 1: do the two CRSs now match?
st_crs(cantons_lux) == st_crs(elev_lux)

# Check 2: are the coordinate ranges now comparable?
st_bbox(cantons_lux)
ext(elev_lux)


[1] TRUE
     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 49540.31  57009.53 105922.01 138631.13 
SpatExtent : 49072.3397901184, 106196.374340225, 56455.2689687042, 139825.481555346 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)




Show code
# Check 3: look at it
plot(elev_lux)
plot(st_geometry(cantons_lux), add = TRUE, border = "red")











Show code
# The zonal mean now works: one number per canton
good <- extract(elev_lux, cantons_lux, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
cantons_lux$elev_mean <- good$elevation

# Check 4: no missing values, and plausible elevations (meters)
sum(is.na(cantons_lux$elev_mean))
summary(cantons_lux$elev_mean)


[1] 0
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  239.6   312.9   322.3   339.7   374.2   467.1 








WarningLabeling is not converting




st_transform() converts: the numbers change
st_set_crs() / st_crs(x) <- ... only relabels: the numbers stay
Relabel only when a file has no CRS and you know what it should be
AI assistants sometimes suggest relabeling as a “fix” for a mismatch:



Show code
# Wrong: claims the degrees are now meters
cantons_relabeled <- st_set_crs(cantons, 2169)


Warning: st_crs<- : replacing crs does not reproject data; use st_transform for that


Show code
st_bbox(cantons_relabeled)


     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 5.744140 49.447807  6.528252 50.181622 



R warns, and the bbox gives it away: still 5.7 to 50.2
In EPSG:2169, numbers that small sit at the grid’s origin: in France, about 120 km southwest of Luxembourg’s center

title: Coordinate Reference Systems
text:
8 Check yourself






Note1. A bounding box reads xmin: 316268 ymin: 4295630 xmax: 334407 ymax: 4318264. Degrees or meters? Projected or geographic?






Meters, so projected: longitudes stop at ±180, latitudes at ±90
Hundreds of thousands and millions look like UTM (this is Washington, DC, in UTM zone 18N)










Note2. extract(r, polygons, fun = mean) returns NaN for every polygon. What’s the likely cause, and how would you check?






CRS mismatch: the polygons and the raster are in different CRSs, so their coordinates don’t overlap and no cells fall inside any polygon
Check: st_crs(polygons) == st_crs(r), compare st_bbox() with ext(), and plot the raster with the polygons on top
Fix: st_transform() the polygons to the raster’s CRS










Note3. You need a 1 km buffer around each TRI facility in Baltimore. An AI writes st_transform(tri, 2263), then st_buffer(tri, 1000). Look up EPSG:2263. What’s wrong?






It’s NAD83 / New York Long Island (ftUS): the wrong place, and the units are US feet
So st_buffer(tri, 1000) makes 1,000 ft buffers (about 305 m), not 1 km
Baltimore is outside its area of use, so distortion is larger too
Better: 26985 (Maryland, meters) or 26918 / 32618 (UTM 18N)










Note4. TRI facilities are in EPSG:4326 and tracts in EPSG:4269, about a meter apart. What happens if you st_join() them without transforming?






Loud: st_join() stops with st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE
sf requires identical CRSs and can’t judge whether a meter matters for your question
Fix: transform one to match the other (or both to a projected CRS you’ll measure in)
Compare with extract() in section 1, which failed silently

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
text:
Today

Explain autocorrelation in time and in space
Explain why autocorrelated samples produce confidence intervals that are too narrow
Tell a sampling design that adds information from one that repeats it
Recognize the fix in R: a model that knows the data are correlated

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
text:
1 Near things are more alike

Tobler’s first law: “Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things”
In time: a warm afternoon predicts a warm evening. One hour later, you learn almost nothing new
In space: a sensor predicts its neighbor down the street. A second sensor there adds little
This is autocorrelation: a variable correlated with itself at nearby times or places

The usual confidence interval for a mean is
\[\bar{x} \pm t \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

The \(\sqrt{n}\) assumes each observation brings new, independent information
lm(), t.test(), and most AI-written code use this formula by default
When observations repeat each other, the formula counts the same information many times

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
section: 2 In time: a lake temperature logger

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
section: 4 Why it happens: effective sample size
text:
4 Why it happens: effective sample size
Two things go wrong at once:

The \(\sqrt{n}\) is too generous. Correlated observations overlap in what they tell you. The effective sample size \(n_\text{eff}\) is smaller than \(n\)
\(s\) is too small. Clustered points see only a slice of the variability (the red dots cover a sliver of the lake’s range)

For readings in a time series where each one correlates \(\rho\) with the next (an AR(1) process), a common approximation is
\[n_\text{eff} \approx n \, \frac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho}\]



Correlation between neighbors (\(\rho\))
20 readings are worth about




0
20


0.5
7


0.8
2


0.99 (one hour apart in the lake)
about 1




The “worth about” tile in each widget estimates the same idea from the simulations
Evenly spaced readings over the whole summer can do better than random, because they never bunch up (try “3 days” vs. “Random times” in the lake widget)

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
section: 5 In R: a model that knows about the correlation
text:
5 In R: a model that knows about the correlation
lm() assumes independent errors. nlme::gls() (generalized least squares) fits the same mean but also estimates how the errors are correlated and widens the CI to match.

In time


Show code
library(nlme)   # gls() and correlation structures; ships with R
library(MASS)   # mvrnorm(), to simulate a correlated surface; ships with R




Show code
# Small helper: one row per model with the estimate, the 95% CI, and the
# CI's width, so the two models are easy to compare at a glance
ci_table <- function(...) {
  models <- list(...)
  rows <- lapply(models, function(m) {
    ci <- confint(m)[1, ]
    c(estimate = unname(coef(m)[1]), lower = unname(ci[1]),
      upper = unname(ci[2]), width = unname(ci[2] - ci[1]))
  })
  round(do.call(rbind, rows), 2)
}




Show code
# Simulate 60 daily lake readings with day-to-day correlation 0.7.
# The true long-run mean is 22 °C.
set.seed(42)
n_days <- 60
temp <- 22 + as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7), n = n_days,
                                  sd = 1.5 * sqrt(1 - 0.7^2)))
lake <- data.frame(day = 1:n_days, temp = temp)




Show code
# Diagnose first: the autocorrelation function (ACF).
# Bars beyond the blue dashed lines = correlation at that lag.
acf(lake$temp, main = "Lake temperature: autocorrelation by lag (days)")











Show code
# Naive: assumes the 60 days are independent
m_lm <- lm(temp ~ 1, data = lake)

# Aware: each day's error is correlated with the previous day's (AR(1))
m_gls <- gls(temp ~ 1, data = lake, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ day))

# The two models side by side
ci_table(lm = m_lm, gls = m_gls)


    estimate lower upper width
lm     21.78 21.37 22.19  0.82
gls    21.63 20.42 22.83  2.41



Nearly the same estimate (gls() gives less weight to runs of correlated days), but compare the width column: the gls() CI is about three times wider
gls() estimated the day-to-day correlation itself (printed as Phi in summary(m_gls))



In space


Show code
# Simulate 80 sensors in 4 clustered neighborhoods of a 40 x 40 km region.
# Temperatures are correlated with distance (exponential, range 6 km).
# The true mean is 31 °C.
set.seed(7)
n <- 80
centers <- cbind(runif(4, 5, 35), runif(4, 5, 35))
xy <- centers[rep(1:4, each = 20), ] + matrix(rnorm(2 * n, sd = 1.5), ncol = 2)
Sigma <- 1.5^2 * exp(-as.matrix(dist(xy)) / 6)   # covariance by distance
sensors <- data.frame(x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2],
                      temp = 31 + mvrnorm(1, rep(0, n), Sigma))




Show code
# Naive
s_lm <- lm(temp ~ 1, data = sensors)

# Aware: errors correlated by distance (exponential decay with x-y distance)
s_gls <- gls(temp ~ 1, data = sensors, correlation = corExp(form = ~ x + y))

# The two models side by side
ci_table(lm = s_lm, gls = s_gls)


    estimate lower upper width
lm     31.57 31.31 31.84  0.54
gls    31.70 30.47 32.93  2.46



The lm() CI misses 31. The gls() CI, more than four times wider, contains it
corExp(form = ~ x + y) needs projected coordinates (meters or km), not degrees (Session 4)
Tools for measuring spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I, variograms) come in a later session

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
section: 6 Closing the loop: naive vs. honest CIs

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
text:
7 In your code








Question
Function
What to look for




Are my observations correlated in time?
acf(resid(model))
Bars past the blue lines at lag 1, 2, …


…in space?
Moran’s I, variogram (later session)
Similar values near each other


Fit a mean or trend that allows for it (time)
gls(y ~ x, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ t))
A wider, more honest CI


…(space)
gls(y ~ x, correlation = corExp(form = ~ x + y))
Same; coordinates must be projected


Avoid it by design
Spread samples out in time and space
Gaps longer than the correlation distance




AI check: when AI code reports a CI or p-value from lm() on a time series or on clustered points, ask: are these observations independent?
Autocorrelation rarely produces errors. It produces confident wrong answers

title: Autocorrelation and Overconfident Estimates
text:
8 Check yourself






Note1. One air-quality monitor logs PM2.5 every hour for a year (8,760 readings). t.test() gives a mean of 9.1 ± 0.04 µg/m³. Is ± 0.04 believable?






No. Hourly readings from one monitor are strongly autocorrelated: pollution episodes last days
The effective sample size is far below 8,760, so the true uncertainty about the annual mean is much larger
Check with acf(); fit with gls(..., correlation = corAR1()), or average to daily or weekly values first and check those too










Note2. You can afford 50 soil samples to estimate county-wide soil carbon. Design A: 50 samples in one farm. Design B: one sample in each of 50 farms across the county. Which CI can you trust?






B. Its samples are far apart, so they’re close to independent and represent the whole county
A’s samples describe one farm. Its CI will be narrow and, for the county, very likely wrong (like the 5 km sensor cluster)










Note3. Does autocorrelation make the estimate itself wrong, or only its CI?






Mostly the CI. In both widgets, the misses scatter above and below the truth, so the estimate isn’t biased on average
But any one clustered estimate can be far off, and the narrow CI hides that
If the clusters are placed non-randomly (e.g., volunteers only in cool, leafy neighborhoods), you get bias on top of overconfidence










Note4. An AI fits lm(temp ~ year) to 40 years of monthly temperatures and reports a warming trend with p < 0.001. What do you ask before believing the p-value?






Are the residuals autocorrelated? Check acf(resid(model))
If yes, refit with gls(temp ~ year, correlation = corAR1()) and compare
The trend may still be real, but the p-value from lm() overstates the evidence, for the same reason the CIs above were too narrow
